content: If dispersible fixed-dose combination formulations are unavailable and oral liquid formulations must be used, it is recommended to transition children to solid oral dosage forms as soon as feasible. When children are required to use adult formulations, meticulous attention must be paid to avoid both underdosing and overdosing. The use of functionally scored tablets is preferred to ensure accurate dosing, particularly when adult dosage forms are employed. Splitting unscored tablets should be avoided, as uniform distribution of the active pharmaceutical ingredient cannot be guaranteed in fragmented tablets. Certain tablets, such as heat-stable formulations of lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or atazanavir (ATV), are manufactured using specialized embedded matrix technology (proprietary melt extrusion) to stabilize heat-labile drug molecules. These tablets must not be cut, split, dissolved, chewed, or crushed, as their bioavailability may vary significantly if not swallowed whole. Dosing regimens should aim to avoid differences between morning and evening doses whenever possible. Children should be weighed at every clinical visit, and their medication doses should be adjusted as they grow or experience changes in weight. National treatment programs should consider the regulatory and local availability status of specific dosage forms when developing treatment recommendations for children. Ongoing research is being conducted to establish dosing guidelines for antiretroviral (ARV) medications in newborns, infants, and young children. Age-specific indications for each drug are based on current evidence and will be updated as new recommendations emerge. For infants younger than 4 weeks, dosing adjustments are necessary due to their reduced ability to metabolize and excrete medications. For infants aged at least 4 weeks but weighing less than 3 kg, the immaturity of renal and hepatic elimination pathways is less concerning, but uncertainties remain regarding appropriate ARV dosing for preterm and low-birth-weight infants. Efavirenz (EFV) is not recommended for children younger than 3 years or weighing less than 10 kg. More data are urgently needed to inform recommendations for EFV use in this age group. Atazanavir (ATV) is approved for use in children aged 3 months and older. Single-strength ATV capsules should always be co-administered with ritonavir (RTV) 100 mg across all weight bands. The ATV powder formulation allows administration to infants and children as young as 3 months. For children weighing 5–10 kg, 200 mg of ATV powder (4 packets, 50 mg per packet) should be administered with 80 mg of RTV oral solution (5 mL). Tenofovir (TDF) is approved for use in children aged 2 years and older, with a target dose of 8 mg/kg or 200 mg/m² (maximum 300 mg). The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group has harmonized TDF dosing with WHO weight bands to reduce the number of strengths required for production. Dosing ensures that children do not receive more than 25% above the maximum target dose or more than 5% below the minimum target dose. Nevirapine (NVP) dose escalation with a half-dose for 2 weeks when initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) is still recommended to mitigate toxicity from high initial NVP levels. However, secondary analysis from the CHAPAS-1 trial suggests that younger children may have a lower risk of toxicity, and starting with a full dose may be considered. More definitive evidence is expected from ongoing trials. Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) liquid formulations require a cold chain for transport and storage. Heat-stable LPV/r tablets must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. LPV/r pellets should not be used in infants younger than 3 months. Raltegravir (RAL) granules are approved for use in children as young as 4 weeks, but their feasibility and acceptability in resource-limited settings remain under investigation. Concerns have been raised about administration challenges in such settings. The bioequivalence of RAL chewable tablets dispersed in liquid is being explored, and further guidance will be provided as additional evidence becomes available. There is limited experience with initiating treatment in newborns living with HIV who are less than 2 weeks old. Pharmacokinetic data to inform accurate dosing for drugs other than zidovudine (AZT) are scarce during this period of rapid renal and hepatic maturation. LPV/r solution should not be given to infants younger than 2 weeks, making HIV treatment management in newborns particularly challenging. Reliable pharmacokinetic data for preterm infants are available only for AZT, with uncertainties in dosing for NVP and lamivudine (3TC). LPV/r solution should not be administered to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age. In recent years, improved ARV formulations, such as dispersible, scored fixed-dose combination tablets, have replaced traditional liquid formulations, simplifying HIV care delivery for children in low-income settings. However, the proliferation of options has led to a multiplicity of formulations across regimens and weight bands, complicating procurement and supply chain management. The Interagency Task Team on the Prevention and Treatment of HIV Infection in Pregnant Women, Mothers, and Their Children provides formulary guidance to programs on selecting optimal ARV drugs for children based on robust criteria. The optimal formulary currently includes nine products delivering recommended firstand second-line regimens across all pediatric weight bands. This formulary is routinely revised to align with current WHO guidelines and available products. Programs are encouraged to procure pediatric dosage forms included in the IATT Optimal Pediatric ARV Formulary. The Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group and the Pediatric Antiretroviral Drug Optimization groups continue to emphasize the urgent need for fixed-dose combination formulations to provide recommended first-line regimens, such as LPV/r-containing solid forms for younger children and EFV + abacavir (ABC) + 3TC fixed-dose combinations for children aged 3–10 years. The availability of co-formulated ATV/r and darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) in heat-stable fixed-dose combinations is critical for facilitating treatment sequencing and scaling up secondand third-line treatments. WHO will continue to work toward simplifying prescribing, dispensing, and dosing guidance while collaborating with pharmaceutical manufacturers and other partners to develop practical recommendations for formulations required to safely accelerate ART scale-up for children.
